#### 9.7.2 The capture phone surface (2i-F, D175)

Ref data-intake-and-edit-data §5.1 owns what capture DURABLY records and which routes exist; this section owns what the
person holding the phone sees. It is the only surface in this program rendered on a device the
operator does not sit at, and every decision below comes from that.

##### The use scene picks the theme, not the category

The operator dashboard is dark because it lives on a desk. The phone surface is **light**, because
its use scene is somebody standing at a filing cabinet or a front desk with a paper form in one
hand, often under a window. A dark UI at whatever brightness the phone happens to be on is the most
common way a capture flow becomes unreadable at the exact moment it is being used. Nothing is
restyled to achieve this: `tokens.css` already ships both themes behind `data-demo-theme`, so the
phone selects the light theme and spends no new colour. The palette budget, the `--ds-*` layer, and
the tailwind ratchet are unchanged, and no operator surface moves. **Two vocabularies, one fact:**
the attribute VALUE is `light` — stamped on both `<html>` and `<body>` of `capture.html:2, 22`, with
`<meta name="color-scheme" content="light">` beside it — and `Paper Ink` is that palette's product
NAME (`DEMO_THEME_LABEL`, `src/dashboard/ds/theme.ts:45-48`, and the word the parity references
carry). A reader who greps for `paper-ink` in the phone entry finds nothing and should not conclude
the theme is unset.

##### It is ONE page whose bottom bar changes verb

Capture → review/reorder → finalize are three states of one page, not three pages and not a wizard.
The task is short, the durable session means a reload lands exactly where the operator was, and a
step indicator would spend the top of a small screen narrating a sequence the bottom bar already
states. The action bar is pinned in the thumb zone and is the only place a primary action ever
appears; what changes between states is its verb, not its position.

##### Order is meaning, so it is a numeral and a button — never a drag

Every photograph tile carries its page number as a large real numeral, because the durable record
enforces contiguous ordinals and the bundle IS the order. Reordering is explicit ▲/▼ controls, not
drag: a drag target inside a scrolling list on a touch screen is the classic failure mode, it
cannot be half-performed with a keyboard, and it announces nothing to a screen reader. Buttons are
reachable, announceable, and each one is a complete act.

##### The camera is the platform's, not ours

Photographs are taken through a real `<input type="file" accept="image/*" capture="environment">`
inside a `<label>` — the same real-input-in-a-label pattern the `Dropzone` primitive established
(D173). Building a viewfinder would mean re-implementing focus, exposure and orientation worse than
the phone already does, on the one surface where a bad photograph is the whole failure.

##### A failure is the server's own sentence, in reserved space

The error region is always in the DOM with its height reserved, so a refusal never jumps the layout
under a thumb that is already moving. It is a `role="alert"` and it renders the server's message
VERBATIM — the kernel's refusal, the projector's failure, the named upload rejection. The phone
composes no prose of its own and swallows no catch: the operator holding the phone is the person who
has to choose between Retry Finalize and Discard, and "something went wrong" decides nothing for
them. Colour is never the only carrier.

##### The QR is the operator's half, and the token is minted once and bounded by TTL

Start Capture is a small control inside the existing dashboard. It calls the loopback-only session
route and renders the returned `phoneUrl` as an inline-SVG QR built by `src/domain/qr-code.ts` — a
pure encoder rather than a dependency, so the payload never leaves the process. The raw token is
MINTED once and rendered once: the durable row holds only its digest, and the URL carries the token
in the FRAGMENT, which no server sees. A refused ingress renders its `message` and `remediation` in
place of the QR, because "capture is unavailable" without the reason is a dead end an operator
cannot act on.

**Minted once is not USED once, and the difference matters to whoever holds the phone.** This
subsection read *"the token exists once"* until 2026-08-21 and was being read as single-use. The
phone presents the token on EVERY request and the server resolves it fresh each time —
`resolveToken` digests it, finds the session, expires it if overdue and stamps the active budget on
first touch (`src/server/dashboard/commands/capture-service.ts:221-259`). What bounds it is TIME:
`preConnectTtlMs` (15 min by default) from creation, then `activeIdleTtlMs` (1 h) from the phone's
first connect (`src/domain/config/schema.ts:265-266`). Every way a token can fail to name a live
session — unknown, malformed, expired, discarded — answers identically, because a difference there
is an enumeration oracle on a public origin (D174).

**Where the control actually lives.** *"A small control inside the existing dashboard"* is as-built
only inside the intake takeover's empty or refused dropzone state (`intake.tsx:1182-1206`), and it
VANISHES once a session loads. So the phone path is reachable exactly when the operator has already
opened intake and has no file — which is the right moment, and is narrower than this paragraph
reads. A second entry point is a surface decision nobody has made; it is recorded here rather than
implied away.

##### As-built notes (2026-08-09)

- **The phone is a SEPARATE Vite entry**, `capture.html` over `src/dashboard/phone/`, not a route in
  the operator SPA. Serving the operator bundle over a public tunnel would ship the whole operator
  UI to the phone origin, and no route filter can un-send bytes. `build.manifest` is emitted so the
  ingress allowlist is generated from the phone entry's own asset closure rather than hand-listed.
  `dashboard-wire-boundary` now walks **every** `*.html` entry under `src/dashboard`, not just
  `index.html` — otherwise a second entry would silently escape D120's Node-built-in check — and a
  new arm proves the phone closure reaches no operator surface, client, or app module.
- **One transport owner per bundle.** `provider-capability-boundary` pinned `fetch` to
  `src/dashboard/client/**`; the phone legitimately needs its own, so
  `src/dashboard/phone/capture-client.ts` is named as the phone bundle's single transport owner
  rather than the rule being relaxed. Its error path returns a `CapturePhoneError` that names why a
  body was unreadable — the `fail-loud-catch-default` ratchet caught a `.catch(() => undefined)`
  there and was right to.
- **The camera stays the primary control even after the first photograph**, and Review is the quiet
  one on the left. Promoting Review was a hazard, not a taste question: Review and Send would then
  both be "primary, on the right", so a second tap from a thumb already travelling would finalize
  the bundle.
- **Motion is the house language, not a phone dialect.** The one authored moment — a photograph
  settling into the list — uses `--ds-dur-enter` and `--ds-travel-md`. An invented
  `--ds-phone-*` pair differing by 30ms and 2px would have been a second motion language that also
  needed its own `prefers-reduced-motion` block to stay honest; the house tokens already collapse.
  Press feedback is `active:scale-[0.97]`, not a 1px translate: a finger COVERS a 48px control, so
  the only visible feedback is at its edges.
- **Red is reserved for Discard.** Per-tile Remove was `danger`-toned, which put three red controls
  down the reorder list — louder than Send, inverting the attention ladder the token file is
  explicit about.
- **Parity: 15 references added** (five states × pixel/a11y/provenance) at one phone viewport in
  their own block, so the operator corpus is not multiplied. **12 moved, none silently**: the
  `intake-upload` triples, because the QR start control lives on that surface; the a11y diff is
  exactly the three lines it adds.
- **Pre-existing defect found and NOT fixed here:** the intake takeover renders a dark shell under
  the light theme, leaving the dropzone heading near-invisible. It is identical in the committed
  baseline and is a sibling of the `paper-ink`-renders-dark residual already deferred to 2j's corpus
  work; fixing it here would re-freeze references for a reason unrelated to capture.

### 9.8 Settings and the storage doctor

<!-- roadmap: p2-2j -->
<!-- roadmap: def-settings -->
<!-- roadmap: def-retention -->

A dashboard-only square: `ref frontend-backend-integration` §5.1 has no counterpart, because
Settings issues no command. Three checklists reach it and none of them opens here — `p2-2j`'s is at
§2.5 (the boot interlock, the backup cadence, the doctor, D181's restore and the process locks),
`def-settings`' at §2.4 (the ONE deferred kernel arm), and `def-retention`'s at §2.1 (the sweep and
the backup path). This section owns what the operator SEES of all that.

**What it is.** The gear in the top bar, opening the sections the SERVER lists. There is exactly
one today — `settingsSections: [{ id: "storage", label: "Storage", revision: 1 }]`
(`src/server/dashboard/queries/bootstrap.ts:122`) — and the surface renders the server's list rather
than its own, so a section this build cannot draw says so BY NAME instead of disappearing. A missing
section is indistinguishable from a section nobody added, and only one of those is a defect.

**Nothing here saves anything, and that is a deferral rather than an omission.** `apply-settings` is
the one command arm the kernel declares and refuses (§2.4, `{#def-settings}`), so Storage is
read-only health and no control on the page pretends otherwise — there are no disabled inputs
waiting for a backend, because a disabled control still claims the act exists.

**Two readings, at two costs.** The **at-rest summary** rides the bootstrap every view already has
(`authority`, `backup`, `checkedAt`) — that is what the gear's attention dot is computed from
(`storageNeedsAttention`: authority not healthy, OR backup not current). The **doctor** is a
deliberate press: `buildStorageDoctor` runs the read-only inspection on demand
(`src/server/dashboard/queries/storage.ts`) and returns authority state, pending durable work,
byte-re-verified backup health, the restore candidates and — beside them — what the live backup
SERVICE last did. That last field exists because the on-disk view cannot see a failure: a backup run
that threw leaves no manifest for the doctor to find, so the process that owns the cadence has to
say so itself (`never-run` | `ok` | `failed`, each with its reason).

**The surface lists restore candidates and cannot restore.** D181's offline restore requires a
one-time stopped-system proof derived from the runtime lock snapshot, and the dashboard is one of
the processes that proof is about — so the act is `cli storage restore` and the page's job is to
tell the operator which candidate is `verified-compatible`, which is `invalid` and why. A button
here would have to either fabricate the proof or fail every time it was pressed.

**D222 — the band was narrowed to the one state that stops the work.** `StorageBanner` renders on
EVERY view (it is mounted above the takeover switch, so the queue, intake, archive, explorer,
catalog and Activity all carry it) and it now appears for **unreachable authority only**. A stale or
missing backup does not stop runs or writes and §2.6 has always named it a `storage` NOTIFICATION,
so it reaches the operator as a durable inbox row plus the gear's dot instead of a band over
everything. The authority case stays a band for a structural reason rather than a volume preference:
**the inbox is an authority table, so an authority that cannot be written cannot record a
notification about its own death.** When both are true the band prints both sentences, authority
first, because that is the one that changes what happens next.

**The band is a HAZARD, which is one of D24's two exemptions.** It names the state, the ONE
consequence that changes what the operator should do next, and the route to the doctor. No third
sentence, no disclosure list, no defence of the design — and every word of it is derived from facts
the bootstrap actually serves, which is why the ported demo's two "what still works / what is
blocked" lists were not ported with it.

### 9.9 The shell — top bar, worker cards, keys, theme

<!-- roadmap: track-c -->

A dashboard-only square: `ref frontend-backend-integration` §5.1 has no counterpart, because the
shell issues no commands of its own. It is the frame every other square renders inside, and it owns
four things nothing else can: the status bar, the workflow rail, the layout grid, and the ONE clock.

The `p1-spine` checklist lives at §1 and the `dash-defaults` one at §9.3; this section adds neither.
Its own block is `track-c`'s, which is the wave-2 connection proof — three of that proof's four
defects were presentation, and two of them are here.

#### The layout is a GRID, and inside the detail region a switch keys on the COLUMN

The detail region is three columns: **queue · centre · context rail**. The split is by reading
pattern (§9.3.1) — live state in the centre, reference in the rail — and **a decision and a failure
never sit behind a collapse control or a lone tab**: `Waiting on you` and `Failed` are the only two
states allowed to shout. The rail collapses to a labelled spine that says what is inside it
(`Context · 9 data · 6 captures`, `--ds-w-context-spine`), with the collapsed preference applied only
above the three-column threshold.

| Width | Layout |
|---|---|
| **< 1180** | one scrolling stack — shape, then detail, then context. The rail degrades to a section, never to nothing. |
| **≥ 1180** | queue `--ds-w-side-panel` (**376px**), a fixed track, + a detail cell taking `minmax(0,1fr)`. |

The **queue and the rail share ONE resting width** and neither side panel grows independently at
wider viewports, so the centre stays the largest column at every size. 376 is 28px wider than the
former 348px rail and narrower than either former queue width, which is what buys the centre back
the room the 400/470 analysis was fighting over.

**The detail cell's own split is a CONTAINER query, not a window one** — `@min-[868px]/detail` and
`@min-[1068px]/detail`, derived as 1280−412 and 1480−412 (`layout-metrics.ts`). The distinction is
the whole point and this doc used to state the principle and then leave window numbers in the table:
the same 1280px viewport gives the centre 414px with the rail open and 728px with it collapsed, so a
viewport media query fires at the wrong moment in both directions. (Caught in the act: the two
`Write parked` resolutions were being forced side by side into a 414px column, each a ~200px box
holding a two-line sentence about whether a real UCPath termination exists.) Only the shell grid
itself is a window query, at `min-[1180px]`, because the window is genuinely what it measures.

**Grid, not flex, is normative — it is what makes the empty case impossible.** The region was
authored as two `flex-1` children. `flex-1` distributes free space only among children that EXIST,
so with no run open the second child was not rendered, nothing claimed the space, and the queue
panel — a flex item with no width — shrank to its content. At 1440×900 that left a ~470px column of
rows and **~950px of empty black** in the middle of the surface this product is named after, at
every viewport since 1i-spine, through a dozen green gates and a frozen reference corpus that
photographed it. A grid cannot fail that way: its tracks exist whether or not anything is placed in
them. And **nothing selected is a STATE** — `No run open`, owing its three things and no more — not
an absent element. It is the same defect class as D187's two-pixel panel (§9.3), found the same way.

*(Measured effect of the reading-pattern split at 1280×720, kept as the record: chrome above the
panels 190px → 117px; each panel 469px → 542px tall; the tab body 123–215px → 213–335px. The
superseded 400/470 numbers and the reasoning that produced them are in
`history/superseded/2026-08-20-dashboard-surfaces-shell-widths.md`.)*

#### The status bar: `All`, a composite, then every individual status (D18)

One row: an **`All`** pill, then a composite **`Needs you`** pill (= the two statuses that mean a
human is blocking), then each individual status. **No status is hidden.** The bar answers *is
anything on me?* first and *what is everything doing?* second. Counts are the same server-side
projection that feeds the queue rows (§2.2); the composite is a sum of projected buckets, **never a
second count path**.

A **zero-count status pill recedes**: it drops its border, its fill and its label down to an icon and
a faint `0`, keeping its slot, its click target and its full accessible name (`Done with warnings` is
130px of bar at rest; at zero it is 34px).

**The gate BANNER that this loudness principle first produced is deleted, and must not be restored on
principle.** The pill model is untouched; what was overridden is the run-detail expression of *the
decision is the loudest thing*. The decision now lives inline in the log stream at the point it was
reached, the panel header keeps a one-line state plus its action, and a small dismissable notice
appears only while a decision is outstanding **and not visible** (an IntersectionObserver on the
decision's anchor; dismissal is per row+tab and re-arms on either change, so a dismissed reminder can
never become an unreachable decision). **Why this is not a loss of loudness:** the decision was being
rendered TWICE — the banner above the tabs and, at the moment it occurred, the same title, copy and
buttons inline in the stream. Removing the banner removed a duplicate, not information; verified on
both the write-parked and identity-approval runs before the deletion. Two bands saying the same thing
is how a dense panel teaches an operator to skim past both.

Recorded with it, because they close the same *can the record hide?* question: a failed run opens on
Logs rather than Review, so the failure record cannot hide behind a tab; and the failure's
write-state sentence — the difference between a safe retry and a duplicate termination — renders
unconditionally in the stream, never behind a disclosure. Only diagnosis may sit behind one.

#### Two `Done`s, three visible channels, and one that is not visible at all (D22 + D126)

The quietest status renders as a green **`Done`** with no icon. The qualifier was doing two jobs
badly: it made the quietest status the longest label in the vocabulary, and beside `Done with
warnings` it asked the operator to work out whether *that* one was verified too. Then the operator
directed that `doneWarnings` also draw the bare word `Done` — the long label shoved the run title off
the row header, beside a count chip that already named the warning. **Both terminal dones now draw
the same word, on purpose, at the operator's direction, and the visible design is settled and not to
be relitigated.**

What separates them on screen is **icon + colour + the count chip**: `doneWarnings` draws an amber
warning triangle carrying its warning count beside an amber-tinted pill, `verifiedDone` the bare word
on a solid green fill. Two visible non-textual channels plus the count, not hue alone.

**And a third channel that is not visible at all.** Because the drawn word stopped distinguishing
them, `StatusFilters` rendered two controls whose accessible names were both `"Done — n"`, and the
queue rows both ended `"— done"`. The defect was assistive-technology ONLY, so only the non-visual
channel was fixed: `DsStatusSpec` gains an optional `accessibleLabel` that is **never rendered**;
`dsStatusText` stays the visible word; `dsStatusAccessibleName` returns `accessibleLabel ?? label`
and is what **every** `aria-label` naming a status must use. Only `doneWarnings` sets one today —
`"Done with warnings"`. The three collisions are closed at their name sites (the filter pill, the
queue row and member line, and `StatusDot`, whose `role="img"` name is all an assistive technology
gets because a dot draws no word at all), never by lengthening a drawn string.

**The pixels are unchanged, and that is verified rather than asserted:** re-freezing the parity
corpus after the change rewrote 56 `.a11y.yml` references and **zero** `.png` files, with every
visible text node byte-identical. **The rule this generalises to:** when two statuses deliberately
share a visible word because a non-textual channel carries the difference, that channel must have an
assistive-technology counterpart. Hue, a glyph and a count chip have none; a future status that
shortens its word owes one too.

The guarantee is structural rather than textual and the shortening is not a weakening: the verdict is
still reachable only via read-back, the receipt still shows its read-back checks, and the wire keys
stay `verified-done` and `done-with-warnings`. *(The reconciliation debt this entry recorded against
`ref operator-trust` is DISCHARGED — that doc now uses only the wire key `verified-done` and never
the drawn label. Row-model D9's long-label sentence is §9.10's to carry.)*

**One correction the audit forced.** D12, D18, D22 and D23 all name the status **`Waiting on you`**;
the drawn word is **`Review`**. `Needs you` survives only as the composite pill and the queue BAND
label. The code's behaviour is the short word, and whether the doc's vocabulary or the drawn one is
authoritative is an operator call (`{#operator-calls}`), like D12's undrawn gate age beside it
(§9.2).

#### The workflow rail lists main workflows only (D219 → D220 → D241)

#### A live elapsed TICKS, from ONE calibration against the server's instant (D256)

**What was wrong.** `useBootstrap` fetches once, and `boot.serverClock.now` — the instant that ONE
fetch carried — was the only value the queue row's in-flight timer, the gate-age pill, the session
footer and the worker cards computed against. Every live elapsed on the dashboard was frozen at page
load. The proof measured it twice over: a parked run displayed **`0s` for more than two minutes** (the
tab had loaded at 15:03:32, the run started at 15:12:17, so the difference was negative and the clamp
made it a plausible zero), and a plain reload at 15:15:15 made the same row jump to **`2m 54s`** —
exactly `bootstrapInstant − startedAt` — and freeze again. A terminal row was unaffected, because
D124 already made its duration two served instants; so this was invisible on every settled run and
wrong on every run an operator is actually watching.

- **The server's instant stays the authority, and the browser contributes only elapsed.**
  Substituting the browser's wall clock is what D124 forbids, and a machine whose clock is minutes off
  would print a duration nobody can act on. What the browser IS authoritative about is how much time
  has passed since that instant arrived, which it reads from the monotonic clock
  (`systemClock.monotonicMs()`, `ref clock-config-secrets`'s single source) — a value an NTP step or a
  user editing the system clock cannot move.
- **One calibration, one value, every consumer.** `src/dashboard/state/served-clock.ts` holds
  `(servedInstant, monotonicMs at receipt)` and derives
  `deriveServedNow = servedInstant + (monotonicNow − monotonicAtReceipt)` on a one-second tick, on
  `visibilitychange` (a backgrounded tab's interval is throttled to about once a minute, and an
  operator returning to it must not read a minute-old age), and on any re-render. `dashboard-app.tsx`
  calls the hook ONCE and passes the result down every path that used to carry the frozen instant,
  **including the keyboard order's own sort key** — the queue's drawn order and the keyboard's
  traversal order must not be able to date one row two ways.
- **No surface reads a clock of its own.** The notification bell's `systemClock.now()` — the last
  display-time wall-clock read in the bundle — is now the same passed-down instant. A second clock on
  one screen is how two chips come to disagree about one gate's age.
- **A backwards elapsed is DRAWN, not clamped.** `elapsedSecondsBetween` returns the SIGNED interval
  and `fmtElapsed` spells a negative one with its sign. The clamp is what let *the clock reading this
  is behind the fact it is reading* wear the shape of *this happened just now*, and those are
  different facts. A sub-second skew still renders `0s` on its own, because `Math.round` of a fraction
  of a second is zero — the signed arm appears only when something is genuinely wrong.
- **Re-calibration is deliberately NOT built, with the trigger that ends the deferral named.** The BFF
  is a loopback singleton (`config/runtime-isolation.json` pins the port; D181's `server` role lock
  admits one holder), so the served clock and the browser's clock are the same machine's clock: there
  is no skew to re-converge on, only the monotonic clock's own drift, immaterial at the seconds
  granularity `fmtElapsed` renders. A server instant on the SSE `health` heartbeat is a wire change
  with a server emitter and two fixture emitters behind it, bought for a skew this deployment cannot
  have. What buys it is `ref frontend-backend-integration` §6.9's deferred exposed path (D189) — the
  day the BFF serves a browser it does not share a machine with. Add the field in that commit.
- **The parity corpus is held by pinning the OTHER half of the clock.** A ticking elapsed dated by real
  browser time would make `45m 0s` and `45m 1s` a coin flip between the run that froze a reference and
  the run that asserts it. `installFrozenMonotonic` freezes `performance.now` before navigation — and
  nothing else, so timers, rAF and CSS animation all still run — which makes the derived instant
  EXACTLY the fixture's served instant, byte-identical to what every existing reference was captured
  against. `assertMonotonicFrozen` proves the page adopted it by reading the clock twice across real
  wall time: D187's rule, applied to a clock instead of a theme.
- **Measured, and then re-measured.** When this landed, the assert lane reported 139 captures failing
  and 12 behaviour cases passing — every capture already failing before the change, because each
  reference's stamped `descriptorHash` predated D226–D255 and the rows had gained D230's `#N` ordinal.
  What mattered then was what the drift was MADE of: across 678 diverging lines, **not one was an
  elapsed**. Track C's ONE deliberate re-freeze has since landed the corpus at **151/151 assert-green**
  over 139 references × 3 files, so the interim number is superseded and only the clock finding it
  supported still stands.

**Wire.** The shell reads the bootstrap document and the SSE day stream and issues no commands of its
own; `ref frontend-backend-integration` §4 owns the bootstrap's shape (including D219's `role` leaf and
D264's moved declaration fields) and §7 the parity lane.

### 9.10 The delegation and row model (row-model D5–D24)

<!-- roadmap: order-4 -->

**What this is.** The operator-ratified presentation series that decided what a ROW is, before any
of it was built. It is a dashboard-only square with no wire counterpart, because it is a vocabulary
rather than a payload: three row types (Run · Group · Member), a `containment` word for how a child
belongs to a parent, and a set of rules for what a group shows at every size.

**Read the whole square with one fact in front of you: the group half is a contract for a shape
nothing can mint.** Every enqueue path in this tree stamps `shape: "single"` — the command kernel,
the capture handoff and the start-plan service alike — and the kernel says so itself in a comment:
*"the coordinator/member fan-out has no runtime yet (nothing mints an `operation` run)."* The
projection, the containment fold, `memberRollup`, `memberPreview`, the member well and the
`run-group` / `run-member` parity references are all real and all fed by hand-composed fixtures.
Building the presentation ahead of the workflows was correct — the shape is what the workflows will
be authored against — and this section says once, here, that it is ahead, rather than repeating the
caveat in each entry.

  demand holding the space of an open one is the same defect inverted. The row's expansion state and
  its explanatory chrome are both projections of settlement, derived in ONE place

#### Two house rules the series settled for every surface

- **D23 — the motion rule is narrowed on purpose.** From *never animate status changes* to **never
  animate ambient status churn; a run that starts needing you may announce itself** — once, on the
  edge. The reasoning, so the narrower form is applied and not merely quoted: a dashboard where
  everything that updates also moves is unreadable exactly when it is busiest, and this one updates
  constantly, so elapsed timers, incrementing counts, background settling and self-initiated re-sorts
  stay STILL — if all of that moved, movement would be unavailable for the one thing that needs it.
  But the two states allowed to shout mark the moment a run stops being background and becomes work,
  and that is precisely the moment the operator is looking somewhere else. **Four constraints keep the
  exception from becoming a licence:** (1) **edge, never state** — it fires on the transition INTO an
  attention status, and a row already waiting when scrolled to does nothing; (2) **never on mount** —
  first sight of a row is not a change; (3) **once, then still** (`ATTENTION_ANNOUNCE_MS`) — nothing
  pulses, repeats or waits to be acknowledged; (4) **only the two loud statuses** — reaching for this
  on a third is the drift, and the answer is no. Implemented once (`useAttentionAnnounce`); never
  re-derived at a second call site. This entry is authority for exactly the attention edge and nothing
  more.
- **D24 — a professional dashboard does not explain itself.** Explanatory prose on a surface is a
  **defect** unless it lives inside an **ⓘ** (a click-to-open popover — reachable by pointer, touch
  and keyboard, costing the surface nothing until asked for). Two exemptions, and only two, because
  neither is explanation: a **refusal**, which must state what was not done and why or the operator
  cannot act on it; and a genuine **hazard** about the run in front of you (a stale checkpoint, a
  staged write, an unresolved park) — those are outcomes, not teaching. **The test:** a sentence on a
  surface must be a fact about the RUN in front of you; a sentence equally true of every run in the
  product is a rule of the product, and a rule of the product is teaching that costs the same pixels
  every time it is drawn whether or not anyone needed it. Operator, verbatim: *"i feel like the
  dashboard right now is bloated with extra information like explanations and descriptions that we
  dont need."* This drove the removal of dozens of strings and the relocation of the rest into ⓘs. An
  **empty state** owes three things and no more: what would be here, why it is not, and what to do —
  it does not owe a defence of the design. The full deletion criteria live in
  `src/dashboard/DESIGN.md`, which is binding on every surface built against this contract.

This document is the production-wiring companion for the rebuild demo. It answers one question:

## 0. Outcome and non-negotiable decisions

<!-- roadmap: phase-1 -->
<!-- roadmap: dash-defaults -->

The optimal foundation is a **typed dashboard backend-for-frontend (BFF) inside the rebuild repo's
own Hono process**, backed by rebuilt authoritative SQLite state and server-side
projections (ref dashboard-surfaces). It is not a separate rebuild service and never shares the legacy Hono
process, routes, middleware, state, port, lock, or browser sessions. It binds loopback only
(`src/server/dashboard/http-server.ts` refuses any other address) over a hand-rolled Node→Hono
bridge, because the chunk-by-chunk pipe is what lets the stream flush without `@hono/node-server`.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  UI["React surfaces\nexact demo composition"]
  CLIENT["one typed dashboard client\nquery · stream · command · artifacts"]
  BFF["Hono dashboard BFF\nstrict boundary schemas"]
  PROJ["server projectors\nqueue · detail · report · archive"]
  AUTH["SQLite authority\ncommands · checkpoints · gates · intents"]
  EVENTS["spans · notes · receipts · captures"]
  EXEC["kernel · workers · drivers"]

  UI --> CLIENT
  CLIENT -->|"GET snapshots"| BFF
  CLIENT -->|"one resumable SSE"| BFF
  CLIENT -->|"one command envelope"| BFF
  BFF --> PROJ
  PROJ --> AUTH
  PROJ --> EVENTS
  BFF --> AUTH
  AUTH --> EXEC
  EXEC --> AUTH
  EXEC --> EVENTS
```

The following are settled:

1. **The frontend renders finished read models.** It does not classify raw tracker rows, infer
   statuses, reconstruct timelines, merge logs, calculate authoritative counts, or decide which
   commands are safe.
2. **One strict client owns all transport per bundle.** Components do not call `fetch` or open a
   stream directly. Query, subscription, command, upload, error normalization, schema parsing,
   reconnect, and cancellation live behind one client boundary — `src/dashboard/client/**` for the
   operator bundle, and `src/dashboard/phone/capture-client.ts` for the phone bundle, which is a
   SECOND browser entry (`capture.html`) that may not reach the operator client at all. One owner
   per bundle, enforced (§8 guard #1).
3. **REST snapshots + one resumable SSE stream + one command route.** This fits the local,
   single-operator product and the current append/project architecture better than GraphQL,
   WebSockets, or a client database. The bulk arm rides its own POST (`/api/v1/commands/bulk`)
   because its result is a per-target VECTOR, not a single result — one envelope shape could not
   carry it (§3.4). Large immutable bytes are meant to use dedicated artifact routes; none is
   served yet (§3.6).
4. **Server facts, client composition.** The server owns facts, state, availability, policy,
   counts, capabilities, and actions. React owns exact layout, focus, responsive behavior,
   animation, local drafts, and the fixed visual mapping from closed wire enums to the approved
   design system.
5. **No optimistic authority.** After a command, the UI may show “request submitted,” but it does
   not locally turn Running into Done, remove a row, resolve a gate, or invent a receipt. The next
   server projection or an authoritative replacement returned with the command result does that.
6. **Build end-to-end slices.** A surface is not complete when its JSX exists. It is complete when
   its schema, projector/query, stream invalidation, command path, degraded/error state, fixture,
   and Playwright visual proof all exist.
7. **The demo remains the visual oracle until parity is complete.** We port its visual language;
   we do not redesign while wiring production data.
8. **The product does not explain itself.** General teaching copy lives in an accessible ⓘ
   popover; only a refusal, a genuine hazard, or a fact about the selected run may consume standing
   surface space (ref dashboard-surfaces D24).
9. **Two repos, one cutover (D88/D89/D93).** The legacy repo's dashboard remains the production UI
   throughout construction, while the rebuild is built in the standalone `hr-automation-rebuild`
   repo. The two share no module graph, build, or process, so neither side *can* proxy, import,
   invoke, or read the other's live state. What still needs deliberate separation — both run on one
   machine — is distinct commands, ports, state/artifact roots, locks, and browser
   profiles/sessions. No workflow or surface flips individually. After the complete integration
   matrix passes, the normal launcher is repointed at the rebuild repo once; the legacy repo is
   preserved wholesale as the rollback asset.

### 1.2 The existing frontend shows why the rebuild needs a BFF boundary

The legacy dashboard had, at the 2026-07-30 survey, **271 frontend files, 30 hook modules, 59 direct
`fetch(` call sites, and 21 Hono route modules**. Those numbers are not defects by themselves; the
coupling is:

- components and hooks know route paths and response quirks;
- multiple polling and SSE resources describe overlapping run state;
- the browser receives tracker-shaped data and owns merge/dedup/classification work;
- startability is split across workflow metadata, `INPUT_RUN_REGISTRY`, `RUN_MODAL_REGISTRY`, and
  workflow-specific routes;
- counts, selected-run snapshots, live entries, logs, screenshots, and failures can arrive from
  different freshness points;
- some backend reads still fall back from SQLite to JSONL, and `/api/entry-data` chooses a
  “richest” row instead of exposing one authoritative detail projection;
- the current SSE hub transports permissive payloads and relies on client JSON parsing/ignoring;
- several product mutations still have one-off route families instead of one audited command
  protocol.

The rebuild must not reproduce this as cleaner folder names. The replacement boundary is one
server-authored product model and one client that parses it. As built, that is **one** transport
module per browser bundle, **36** command actions behind **one** POST, and **zero** handwritten wire
mirrors — the three properties §8's guards hold.

## 2. Production module boundaries

<!-- roadmap: p1-spine -->
<!-- roadmap: track-d -->

The production tree makes the dependency direction obvious. This is the tree **as built**:

```text
src/
├── domain/
│   ├── commands.ts               # the command envelope/result/family/action schemas
│   └── dashboard/
│       ├── bootstrap.ts          # strict wire schemas; zero React/Node imports
│       ├── projection.ts         # dashboard/day/queue/worker-card/status schemas
│       ├── run-detail.ts         # panel kind + section schemas
│       ├── subscription.ts       # hello/snapshot/patch/reset/cursor envelopes
│       ├── artifacts.ts          # refs/manifests, never local paths
│       ├── activity.ts · archive.ts · explorer.ts · storage.ts · advisory.ts
│       ├── actions.ts            # served action descriptors
│       └── primitives.ts         # the shared closed unions (sections, features)
├── server/
│   └── dashboard/
│       ├── routes/api.ts         # the ONE thin parse/host-gate/dispatch boundary
│       ├── queries/              # bootstrap · run-detail · archive · explorer · activity-export · storage · advisory · ui-catalog
│       ├── projectors/           # run-queue-projection · worker-cards · queue-row-actions · run-subject-title
│       ├── commands/             # command-service · start-plan-service · intake-service · capture-service
│       ├── subscriptions/        # dashboard-stream: cursor/ring → SSE envelopes
│       ├── compose.ts            # the composition root
│       └── http-server.ts        # the loopback Node→Hono bridge
└── dashboard/
    ├── app/                      # shell, URL/nav state, global keys, command dispatch, the ONE command-result fold
    ├── client/                   # the operator bundle's only transport
    ├── state/                    # React resource hooks over the client
    ├── ds/                       # the design system: tokens, primitives, the ONE barrel
    ├── surfaces/                 # every operator surface, each paired with a `<surface>-model.ts`
    ├── lib/                      # framework-free helpers
    └── phone/                    # the phone capture bundle: its own entry, its own transport
```

Rules:

- `domain/dashboard/**` (plus `domain/commands.ts`, which is shared with the kernel) exports strict
  zod schemas and inferred types. There is no handwritten duplicate frontend interface (§8 #2).
- Route handlers parse input, call a query/command service, parse output, and return it. They do
  not contain workflow switches or projection logic.
- Projectors never import React. React never imports workflow modules, stores, SQLite, tracker
  readers, or server registries — with the one named exception in §4 (`WORKFLOW_DESCRIPTORS`, D264
  row D11).
- **One transport owner per bundle**: `dashboard/client/**` for the operator app,
  `dashboard/phone/capture-client.ts` for the phone. The phone bundle may not reach the operator
  client, so it needs its own; the principle is unchanged and the guard names ONE file rather than
  the whole `phone/` subtree, so a component reaching for `fetch` still fails (§8 #1).
- Product surfaces may import only strict wire types, the client facade, design-system primitives,
  and pure presentation helpers.
- A `surfaces/*.tsx` or `app/*.tsx` module exports components only; its pure half lives in
  `<surface>-model.ts` (§8 #14).
- The BFF remains in-process. Splitting it into a network service adds failure modes and gives this
  local-first tool no benefit.

**As built, `state/` is half of what this table says it is.** The folder holds React resource hooks
(`use-bootstrap`, `use-dashboard-day`, `use-run-detail`, `client-context`, `served-clock`,
`async-resource`) — the "client-only UI state" half. The **normalized server cache** half was never
built: `async-resource.ts` is the right shape and four callers use it, while the fetch effect is
hand-copied in at least nine other places and 13 of 19 `useDashboardClient` consumers bypass
`state/` entirely. That is Track D row **D6**, and it is named here rather than left for the next
reader to find (`docs/plans/2026-08-20-dashboard-architecture-audit.md` §3.4 M2). Two more Track D
rows amend this section: **D7** splits `LoadedApp` (`app/dashboard-app.tsx`, ~1,100 lines, 18
concerns) along its own seams, and **D8** gives `intake.tsx` and `archive.tsx` the models the
pairing rule assumes and splits the workflow-versioning surface out of the archive file. Their
checklist lives in §7.4's status block, with the rest of the track.

### 3.1 `FrontendBootstrapWire`

<!-- roadmap: p1-spine -->

`FrontendBootstrapWireSchema` — `src/domain/dashboard/bootstrap.ts`. Fetched once at app boot and
refetched when the subscription declares descriptor/config skew.

```ts
interface FrontendBootstrapWire {
  wireVersion: 1;
  appVersion: string;
  descriptorHash: Fingerprint;
  settingsSchemaHash: Fingerprint;
  projectionGeneration: number;
  actor: { id: "local-operator"; label: string };
  serverClock: { now: IsoInstant; zone: "America/Los_Angeles" };
  storage: StorageHealthSummaryWire;
  workflows: WorkflowClientProjection[];
  systemInstances: SystemInstanceProjection[];
  settingsSections: SettingsSectionProjection[];
  featureAvailability: FeatureAvailabilityWire[];
  preflight?: PreflightCheckWire[];
}
```

`actor.id` is the **literal** `"local-operator"`, not a free actor id: this is a single-operator
local tool (D193) and a schema that admitted any slug would be describing a product that does not
exist. `featureAvailability` is closed to `capture | ocr | ai-advisory | archive | workflow-editor`.

`preflight` is the doctor's standing summary — one entry per check, each carrying its verdict, its
detail, the named things its failure **blocks**, an optional remediation, and the instant it was
checked. The Top Bar owns it (§5): the stethoscope carries the worst verdict of the set, its popover
lists the checks, and "Run doctor again" is the paired command. It is **optional and unserved
today** — `buildBootstrap` composes no preflight service — and its absence is declared as
`FrontendBootstrapWireSchema#preflight` in `config/pending-wire-bindings.json` (D184). The surface
renders the whole popover only when the field is present: a doctor indicator over checks nobody ran
would report a pass the server never made. The verdict itself is DERIVED on the client from the
checks (`fail` beats `warning` beats `pass`) and is never a second served field, so the glyph and
the list cannot disagree.

The workflow projection includes label/icon/category/code/version, panel kind, graph summary,
systems, start methods/options/presets, dry-run support or explicit absence reason, input subject,
status/verdict vocabulary, detail capabilities, action policy summary, and source availability.
The client derives navigation from this list; no parallel workflow registry survives — **except the
one named in §4**, which D264 row D11 removes.

**Category GROUPING is served raw and displayed by the client (R2 D17/D18).** The projection carries
each workflow's own `category` id and nothing else about grouping — there is no `workflowCategories`
projection, because the one this wire used to carry invented both of its fields (`label` was
`id.replace(/-/g, " ")`, `order` was the registry's first-seen index), so the Workflow Panel's
headings read `separation` in whatever order a module happened to import. Ref dashboard-surfaces §9.9 is the
owner and it is explicit: *the frontend hardcodes only the display order, membership is the
descriptor's, an unlisted category appends, and an empty category drops.* The heading text and the
order therefore live in `src/dashboard/surfaces/workflow-category.ts`, typed
`Record<WorkflowCategory, …>` so a new category in the descriptor vocabulary fails `tsc` rather than
rendering a hole, and BOTH the Workflow Panel's rail and the Run Modal's picker call its one
`groupWorkflowsByCategory` — two surfaces that once held hand-copied copies of the same rule.

### 3.2 `DashboardDayWire`

<!-- roadmap: p1-spine -->
<!-- roadmap: track-b -->
<!-- roadmap: track-d -->

`DashboardDayWireSchema` — `src/domain/dashboard/projection.ts`. One query provides the selected
day's coherent shell and queue state:

```ts
interface DashboardDayWire {
  day: LocalDate;
  descriptorHash: Fingerprint;
  projectionGeneration: number;
  snapshotCursor: ProjectionCursor;
  monthCounts: readonly DayCountWire[];
  workflowCounts: readonly WorkflowCountWire[];
  statusCounts: readonly StatusCountWire[];
  queueSurfaces: readonly QueueSurfaceWire[];
  workerCards: readonly WorkerCardWire[];
  notifications: readonly NotificationWire[];
}
```

`monthCounts` rides this payload rather than a calendar route: the calendar and the queue below it
are the same fold, so a second endpoint is the second count path D81 forbids.

`QueueSurfaceWire` remains flat. Group/member relationships use ids and `parentRunId`; the client
may join those ids for layout but may not reinterpret containment or status. Counts and rows are
folded from the same projection transaction/generation. The calendar, Workflow Panel, Status Bar,
queue header, and Activity query can therefore never disagree because of different source paths.

**`WorkflowCountWire` carries its own status dimension** — `{ workflowId, count, statusCounts[] }`,
the per-status counts summing to `count` by refinement (R2 D5–D12, R4-1). One `count` per workflow
could not answer the two questions the shell asks of it: the Workflow Panel's `active │ all` column
needs queued + running for THAT workflow, and the Status Bar's pills are scoped to the workflow the
queue below them is showing — so a day-wide fold put `Failed 3` above a queue with no failures. Both
are the same fact at two scopes and both come off this one array, filled in the projector's single
countable loop beside the day-wide totals it must agree with (D81). A client-side fold over
`queueSurfaces` is the second count path that rule exists to delete, and remains forbidden.

**A queue row states its ORDINAL, its CLASS and what it MADE** (D230/D231, 2026-08-19).
`QueueBaseFields` carries `runNumber` — durable on `RunRecord`, assigned per workflow at enqueue,
served with a D133 read-forward absent arm and never derived from a row's position in the day's
array; `priority` — read from the run envelope, which is what D95's `bump` rewrites, and a
deliberate enum mirror of `RunPrioritySchema` kept member-for-member identical by
`wire-connectivity`'s mirror joint (§8 #8) because
`src/domain/run/envelope.ts` is outside the bundle's reach (§8 #13); `containment`
(`root | member | linked`, projected from shape and lineage, with a refinement refusing every
disagreement with `lineage`/`surfaceKind` and no `rejected` arm until a producer writes such a row);
`linkedRuns[]` — each delegated child's id, workflow, label, panel kind and LIVE status, because a
client re-deriving the target's status from `queueSurfaces` is D81's forbidden second path and goes
blank the moment the target sits on another day; `facts[]` — the run's already-derived evidence
receipt's `output`, chipped only where the redacted value is `allowed` and primitive; and
`pipeline[].durationSec`/`executions`, summed over every execution of the node. An operation row
additionally carries `memberPreview`, composed from its members' own served titles. Every one of
these carries its absence as a reasoned arm rather than a zero, an empty band, or a plausible
number.

**A worker card IS the authority lease, joined with what its spans hold open** (D248, 2026-08-20).
`WorkerCardWireSchema` carries `workerId`, `workflowId`, `state`, `directive`, `startedAt`,
`endedAt` + `stopReason`, `currentRun`, `browsers[]`, `leaseVersion` and `revision`. The card SET is
authority's: every live lease is a card, a settled lease is a card while the retained span stream
still names its worker, and a worker the spans name but authority does not is NOT a card — authority
is what says a worker exists. Until D248 the projector derived a worker's phase from whichever rows
happened to be claimed, which is exactly the inference ref execution-and-sessions §3 says the lease exists to make
unnecessary, and it cost three of the six state arms the Session Panel drew: a daemon that had
started and not yet reported read as `idle`, and a worker whose PROCESS DIED was drawn identically
to one the operator had asked to stop.

Four rules travel with it. **`state` and `directive` are separate fields**, because
`src/domain/run/worker.ts` separates them: a command writes what was ASKED and the worker writes
what is TRUE, so folding a pending `pause` into the state word would let a card read `Paused` while
its worker is mid-transaction on a live HR system. **Every arm of both has a producer** — the served
state vocabulary is exactly `starting | idle | working | stopped | failed` (the lifecycle's own
`busy` becomes the card's `working`; its `paused` and `stopping` are NOT mirrored, because nothing
reports them), and the demo's `waiting` arm is gone because this platform gives every worker its own
browser session per system (ref execution-and-sessions §1), so there is no cross-worker lease to wait on and no
holder to name. **`stopped` and `failed` split the terminal lifecycle by its RECORDED reason**
(`operator`/`shutdown` versus `crashed`/`lease-expired`, the latter written by the recovery sweep),
pinned by a refinement — that split is the whole content of `failed`. And **`leaseVersion` is the
lease's row version, never `revision`**, which counts folded span events and is a patch cursor:
binding the Stop control to it would have fabricated the exact fact a version check exists to check.

`browsers[]` is the sessions a worker HOLDS — `{sessionId, system, openedAt}`, started, not yet
closed, keyed by the session id its span path carries — and a settled card holds none, because its
process is gone and its Chromium children went with it. It carries no `health` and no `url`: nothing
in this build probes a live session, so the only verdict available is "never probed" and a six-arm
health enum would be five unreachable arms; and no span, checkpoint or lease records a page address,
so a URL would have to be composed rather than observed. The tile therefore states which system a
session speaks to and how long it has been open, which is what the wire actually knows.

The approved queue contract must include:

- immutable identity, attempt/lineage, actor, descriptor/app/config versions and resolved instance;
- server-resolved title/subtitle/status/live message/run facts;
- final pipeline and open gates;
- member ids/rollups/containment and streamed-record rollups;
- server-authored action descriptors with placement and version/audit tokens;
- `panelKind` plus closed available-section keys;
- evidence/failure/receipt confidence pointers;
- a monotonic `rowRevision` used by commands and patches.

**Every command CASes.** An earlier draft of this list said CAS was enforced only for the four
real-race command families; the schema does not work that way and never did — every family's target
carries a required `expectedVersion`, and the kernel revalidates inside its own transaction (§3.4).

**Track D amends how this payload is CONSUMED, not what it says.** Row **D4** stops the client
re-parsing the whole day on every single-row patch (`client/day-state.ts` runs
`DashboardDayWireSchema.parse` over all rows per patch) and memoizes the three hot panels; at
legacy's real volume — 1,240 rows on the busiest day, 108-member operations — that is the one item
on the audit's list a single operator perceives. Row **D5** bounds the projector's own scans
(`#memberPreview` joins every member to print three; two receipt reads per terminal row). Both
measure and record the numbers §7.4 has been waiting for.

### 3.3 `RunDetailWire` and lazy sections

<!-- roadmap: p1-spine -->
<!-- roadmap: track-b -->

`RunDetailWireSchema` — `src/domain/dashboard/run-detail.ts`. Opening a row fetches one small header
plus only the selected panel section. A terminal 50-person packet must not ship every note, capture,
and facsimile in the day payload.

```ts
interface RunDetailWire {
  runId: RunId;
  rowRevision: number;
  panelKind: "run" | "member" | "review" | "group";
  header: RunIdentityWire;
  timeline: TimelineWire;
  gate: GateDecisionWire;        // present-or-absent IN the union, never an optional field
  outcome: OutcomeWire;          // likewise
  context: ContextSummaryWire;
  availableSections: readonly RunDetailSection[];
}

type RunDetailSection =
  | "logs" | "receipt" | "review" | "people"
  | "context-data" | "context-evidence" | "context-attempts"
  | "failure" | "captures"
  | "parked-write" | "identity-gate";
```

**`gate` and `outcome` are required fields carrying an explicit `{state:"absent", reason}` arm**,
not optional fields. The difference is the whole honesty posture of this wire: an optional field
that is missing cannot say WHY, so a panel drawing nothing could not tell "this run has no gate"
from "the projection failed to look". Every capability on this payload takes the same shape.

The fixed frontend mapping is:

| `panelKind` | Tabs | Always-visible adjacent content |
|---|---|---|
| `run` / `member` | Logs · Receipt | timeline, gate/outcome/failure, Context rail |
| `review` | Review · Logs · Receipt | timeline, gate/outcome/failure, Context rail |
| `group` | People · Logs · Receipt | timeline, gate/outcome/failure, Context rail |

Data lives in the Context rail. Captures live in Receipt and Review where relevant. A backend
capability may make a section empty/absent; it may not silently change the approved composition.

**Four of the eleven section arms have no producer, and each is DECLARED** in
`config/pending-wire-bindings.json` rather than left silent (D184, the D107 pattern one layer up):
`review` and `people` (no registered descriptor declares those panel kinds; the record store is 2h),
`context-evidence` (`buildRunDetail` serves `evidenceFacts: 0` and the evidence service is a later
slice), and `captures` (the section lists artifact refs and **nothing serves artifact bytes** —
§3.6). `wire-connectivity` fails in both directions over that manifest: an undeclared orphan arm, and
a declaration whose binding has become reachable.

Logs are served by cursor-paged GET on the section route as strict note/observed/fence rows; the legacy
`notes` member is an exact compatibility mirror of that page's note rows while the renderer moves to rows.
Review records use stable record ids
and record revisions so one page result can stream without replacing the whole run; People use
stable member ids and pagination metadata for large groups. Receipt, failure, and archive evidence
are immutable once finalized. **The per-run SUBSCRIPTION those three describe does not exist yet** —
the stream emits one topic (§3.5), so a panel follows the day stream's `rowRevision` for its live
key and re-reads the section (D257).

### 3.4 One command protocol

<!-- roadmap: p1-kernel -->
<!-- roadmap: track-b -->
<!-- roadmap: track-d -->

<!-- roadmap: cross-cutting -->

All JSON mutations enter one route (`POST /api/v1/commands`) and one durable command journal. The
schemas are `src/domain/commands.ts`; the kernel is `src/core/command-kernel.ts`, and D113 confines
the journal, the audit and start-plan consumption to it.

```ts
interface CommandEnvelopeFields {
  commandId: CommandId;
  requestedAt: IsoInstant;
  requestedBy: ActorId;
  source: CommandSourceSchema;   // where the request came from
  reason?: string;               // an operator's own words, where a family asks for them
}
// discriminated by a PAIR: `family` (9) × `type` (36), with a per-arm `target` and `payload`
type CommandResult =
  | { state: "applied" | "already-applied"; commandId: CommandId;
      affectedTargets: readonly AffectedTarget[] /* ≥1 */ }
  | { state: "conflict"; commandId: CommandId; currentVersion: number; message: string }
  | { state: "rejected"; commandId: CommandId; code: CommandRejectionCode; message: string };
```

The nine families are `start · intake · worker-browser · settings · version-archive · run · gate ·
notification · capture`, and the 36 actions under them cover: start-run; intake inspect/confirm
mapping/correct row/exclude row/validate/enqueue manifest; worker plan-count/spawn/stop/pause/resume
and browser refresh/reopen; `apply-settings`; version plan/apply/relaunch-archived-run; the run verbs
`retry · cancel · bump · rename · edit-checkpoint · resolve-write-present · resolve-write-absent`;
`resolve-gate`; notification read/unread/snooze; and the seven capture verbs. Dedicated legacy
mutation endpoints are not recreated.

**Every arm CASes on a required `expectedVersion`.** There is no privileged subset: run verbs,
intake, worker, capture, settings and version targets all carry one, and the kernel revalidates the
row inside its own transaction and CASes on what it reads there — so the field states the caller's
BASIS rather than being the check itself.

**A refusal has two arms and both must be handled** — `rejected` (a kernel refusal with one of seven
codes, including D113's `capability-unavailable`) and `conflict` (the CAS refusal carrying the
server's `currentVersion`). `src/dashboard/app/command-result.ts` is the ONE fold that settles them;
D253 (§5.1) is the decision and `command-result-exhaustive` the guard.

**Bulk rides its own route** — `POST /api/v1/commands/bulk`, family `run`, type `retry | cancel |
bump`, a `bulkCommandId`, `targets[≥1]` and a `mode`. It returns one complete per-target vector with
four outcome arms; a partial result can never collapse to one success toast. The `all-or-none` mode
is declared and refuses by name with `capability-unavailable` (D235) — `best-effort` is what runs.
The second route exists because the RESULT shape differs: a vector is not a `CommandResult`, and
widening the single-result union to sometimes be a list would make every caller check.

**Multipart bytes are the exception to the JSON route.** Uploads enter through
`POST /api/v1/intake/files` (which also creates or joins the intake session) and the phone's own
photo routes; the command then references the stored artifact. There is no generic
`POST /api/v1/uploads`.

**Server action descriptors are the only source** for command availability, labels, placement,
confirmation copy, required forms, and revision tokens.

**`apply-settings` is the one command arm that is declared and refused.** It is the sole
`PHASE1_DEFERRED` entry in the kernel: it answers `capability-unavailable` with zero authority
effect, so Settings is read-only in the product today. The family, the target and the atomic N-leaf
payload are already the contract; what is missing is the config-service half
(ref clock-config-secrets §3), which is also what would serve `preflight` and the doctor-rerun
command (§3.1).

**`requestedBy` is not yet enforced, and that is a gap rather than a design.** The contract is that
the client echoes the actor from bootstrap, the server requires it to match the request's identity
checkpoint, then stamps the authoritative actor and acceptance time on the durable command record —
a mismatch rejects, and request-body identity is never trusted. As built, the kernel stamps
`request.requestedBy` verbatim into `resolvedBy` / `plannedBy` / `appliedBy` / `archivedBy` /
`relaunchedBy` and compares an actor id only for notification-row ownership. On a single-operator
loopback tool with one literal actor (§3.1) nothing can currently present a different one; the
contract stands because it is what makes the durable record's actor a fact rather than a claim, and
the enforcement is listed as to-build below.

**A command whose target is not a run is composed beside the composer, not inside it** (D249,
2026-08-20). `composeCommandRequest` is exhaustive over the SERVED row-action vocabulary and every
one of its arms targets a `runId`; the Session Panel's `Stop` targets a worker lease, so widening
the shared `ActionTarget` to hold either would make every run arm accept a target it can never use.
`composeStopWorkerCommand` therefore stands beside it, composes the whole envelope from facts the
card already carries, and has no refusal arm — the two states where stopping is meaningless (a
settled lease, a worker already asked to stop) disable the control AT the card rather than being
discovered after a click. Its `expectedVersion` is the served `leaseVersion`; the kernel revalidates
the lease inside its own transaction and CASes on what it reads there, so the field states the
operator's BASIS rather than claiming to be the check — the shape ref execution-and-sessions §"A capture command's
`expectedVersion` is not a CAS" already ratified.

**A served descriptor may also declare how much CEREMONY its command costs, and a surface obeys it
or refuses (D226, 2026-08-19).** The identity gate is the case that forced the rule: ref write-safety §14.6
risk 1 makes `approvalShape` a SERVER computation precisely so a frontend cannot quietly turn a
risky approval into one click, and the `identity-gate` section serves it beside the packet and both
typed resolutions. Three obligations follow for any surface that renders such a control, and they
generalise to every future server-declared ceremony:

1. **Render the shape the server named, and only that one.** The control for a shape that asks the
   operator to CHOOSE carries no pre-selected option — a pre-selected radio is a one-click approve
   wearing a radio's clothes, which is the downgrade the server-side computation exists to prevent.
2. **A shape this build does not know draws a NAMED REFUSAL and blocks the send.** It may not fall
   back to the cheapest control it does know. A wire value can outrun a bundle — a server upgraded
   ahead of an open tab — and answering under a ceremony nobody implemented is worse than having no
   guard, because the server is still reporting that it asked a question.
3. **The operator supplies only what no served fact carries.** Every other leaf of the payload is
   read off the section — the schema hash, the evidence digest, and the label the server paired with
   each option. A client that derived any of them would be a second implementation of the
   descriptor's identity, and a client that INVENTED one would put a value nobody authored onto a
   durable record. Composition stays in the one composer; the surface hands it the human's answer.

The `RunDetailSectionResponse` arm this is stated over is `identity-gate`; ref write-safety §14.11 owns the
gate's own ceremony table.

### 3.5 Resumable subscription protocol

<!-- roadmap: p1-spine -->
<!-- roadmap: track-c -->

One stream carries closed envelopes (`DashboardStreamEnvelopeSchema`,
`src/domain/dashboard/subscription.ts`):

```ts
type DashboardStreamEnvelope =
  | { type: "hello"; wireVersion: 1; descriptorHash: Fingerprint;
      projectionGeneration: number; cursor: ProjectionCursor }
  | { type: "snapshot"; topic: TopicKey; cursor: ProjectionCursor;
      payload: DashboardTopicSnapshot }
  | { type: "patch"; topic: TopicKey; cursor: ProjectionCursor;
      payload: DashboardTopicPatch }
  | { type: "reset-required"; reason: "cursor-expired" | "generation-changed" |
      "descriptor-changed"; cursor: ProjectionCursor }
  | { type: "health"; state: "live" | "reconnecting" | "degraded" };
```

Rules:

- every envelope parses before entering client state; malformed payload is a visible protocol
  failure, never `console.warn` + ignore;
- cursors are monotonic and delivered as SSE ids; reconnect sends the pair `Last-Event-ID` plus
  `Dashboard-Projection-Generation` (query fallbacks are `cursor` plus `generation`);
- duplicate/current cursors are idempotent; when a HISTORICAL requested cursor cannot be replayed
  from retained history in that exact generation, the server first commits A46's pinned backfill-gap
  notification and only then serves a fresh snapshot;
- a descriptor hash or projection-generation change invalidates affected cached projections;
- queue patches replace one complete surface by `(runId,rowRevision)`; Review patches replace one
  complete record by `(recordId,recordRevision)`; note pages append by stable note id;
- stream payloads signal authoritative changes. They do not carry local UI state or draft edits;
- the server bounds subscriber buffers and tells the client to reset rather than silently dropping
  state-bearing messages.

**The history-gap detector is the replay boundary, not a timer.** `DashboardStreamHub.connect`
requires exact generation-bound cursor evidence before it considers replay. A cursor from another
projection generation — including a held cursor across rebuild or process restart — means the old
ordinal space is no longer comparable, so it receives a fresh snapshot and publishes nothing. A
cursor without generation evidence is equally ineligible. Within one exact generation,
`cursor-expired` means the held cursor predates the replay window and `snapshot-boundary` means a
later full snapshot made the old patch chain unreplayable. Only those two historical-cursor outcomes
publish. A disconnect, timeout, malformed cursor, current or future cursor, cross-generation
cursor, missing generation, ordinary reconnect and subscriber-buffer overflow do not; overflow is
the separate `reset-required` arm.

The hub captures one complete `DashboardDayWire` and derives hello's generation/cursor/hash and the
snapshot envelope from that same object. It awaits the durable publication before exposing the
replacement. If publication itself moves the projection generation or cursor, the captured pair is
discarded and a new hello+snapshot handshake is captured; hello N is never paired with snapshot N+1.

The replacement snapshot establishes a new projection baseline; it does not prove what the operator
missed. Reconnect and resnapshot therefore never clear the durable gap record. Until Track F
ratifies independent reconciliation evidence and a separate resolved transition, that record stays
permanently pinned.

**It is SSE, and it is deliberately not an `EventSource`.** `src/dashboard/client/transport.ts`
speaks the SSE wire format over `fetch` + `ReadableStream`, because `EventSource` cannot set request
headers and the resume contract is the bound `Last-Event-ID` + `Dashboard-Projection-Generation`
pair. The route reads those headers and falls back to `?cursor=&generation=`; generation without a
cursor and every malformed value fail the strict request schema.

**One topic has a producer.** `TopicKeySchema` declares six (`dashboard-day`, `run-detail`,
`run-logs`, `run-review`, `run-people`, `artifact`); the route's topic pattern admits only
`dashboard-day:YYYY-MM-DD` and the hub emits only that topic. Every per-run subscription this
section and §3.3 describe — Review record patches, note-page appends, artifact availability — is
machinery with nothing on the other side of it. **That is the one unserved thing on this wire that
is NOT declared** in `config/pending-wire-bindings.json`, and it should be; it is listed as to-build
in §3's status block. What a panel does instead is D257: it follows the day stream's `rowRevision`
for that run and re-reads the section, so a live thing has a live key.

**What feeds the projector is a disk tail, not an in-process hook (D218).** A worker is a separate
OS process, so `compose.ts` seeds the projection with `rebuildFromJsonl()` at boot — refusing to
start over a degraded projection — and then polls `ingestFromDisk()` on a byte cursor; the command
service ticks the same cursor after its own emissions so an operator's follow-up read never waits
for the poll. The `onEvent` hook that used to feed it is deleted, which is what makes "append first,
fold after" structural.

**Five capability gaps remain in this section, and each has an owner.**

| Capability | State | Owner / trigger |
|---|---|---|
| **Generic artifact resources** | The generic `ArtifactRefWireSchema` / `ArtifactResourceWireSchema` family remains unserved. DCA1's `GET /artifacts/v1/:artifactId` serves exact diagnostic-index-authorized bytes; DCA4's separate archived-capture route serves only frozen archive references. Neither admits arbitrary stored ids or completes the generic gallery. | `legacy-route-files`; the remaining generic resource/captures gallery work keeps its owner |
| **Cross-date run search** — `GET /api/v1/search?q=` | absent. The Top Bar's search filters **the day already served** (`day-search-model.ts`), and the surface says so in its own header rather than implying more. | `legacy-route-search`, D184 → `{#def-search-export}` |
| **The explorer's live-run overlay** — `?runId=` | absent. `GET /api/v1/explorer` serves the static descriptor graph; no overlay parameter exists. | `{#def-explorer-edit}`'s sibling work; recorded here rather than implied by §1.1's row |
| **Excel export** | absent. The one export served is the Activity report as **CSV** (D240). The xlsx sink exists as a retention sink and is uncomposed in production (D164). | `{#def-search-export}` |
| **Settings write / preflight** | `GET /api/v1/settings` and `GET /api/v1/storage/health` are not routes; the facts ride `bootstrap.settingsSections` and `GET /api/v1/storage/doctor`. The write half is §3.4's deferred command arm. | `{#def-settings}` |

Artifacts are fetched through opaque ids with media type, byte length, digest, dimensions/page
metadata, redaction/sensitivity policy, and explicit missing/purged state. The frontend never
receives a local filesystem path and never guesses capture aspect ratio. The generic artifact
family remains unserved. DCA4 serves only an archived capture through the run's immutable archived
record: the resource query finds the exact `(archived runId, artifactId)` tile, builds its read ref
solely from that tile's frozen id/digest/byte length/media type, and verifies all physical bytes
before answering `available` or serving a download. It consults neither a live run nor a current
diagnostic-attachment index. Physical absence is `missing`; a size/digest/read failure is `error`;
an elapsed retention deadline and a missing diagnostic index are neither evidence of a purge. No
durable purge tombstone exists, so `purged` is intentionally not emitted. Frozen capture metadata
and the read-time resource state remain separate wires.

Both DCA4 handlers first require the artifact-store capability to be composed: if it is absent,
they return no-store 409 `SECTION_UNAVAILABLE` before parsing either caller id, even when those ids
are malformed, and perform no archive lookup or byte open. Once the capability is composed, both
routes validate the caller's two ids before archive lookup. The returned row must have the
same run id, a valid strict schema and a matching recomputed archive content digest. Duplicate tile
ids are legal only when their complete byte reference agrees. The resource wire binds its download
URL to its own two ids; it cannot point at another run, artifact, host or path. Resource status uses
verify-only streaming, while each download independently materializes and verifies exact bytes.
The byte response has the frozen media type, exact content length, an id-only attachment filename,
`X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, and `Cache-Control: no-store`. Resource responses are also no-store.
Unsupported Range answers 416 with `Content-Range: bytes */<verified length>` only AFTER verification.
Both routes remain outside the capture Host's closed allowlist (the standard not-found response).

| DCA4 read result | Resource route | Byte route |
|---|---|---|
| Artifact store not composed (even with malformed caller ids) | No-store 409 `SECTION_UNAVAILABLE`, before id parsing; zero archive lookups/byte opens | same |
| Malformed caller id, after artifact-store capability is composed | 400 `SCHEMA_INVALID` | same |
| Archive/tile or frozen metadata absent | 404 `TARGET_NOT_FOUND`, zero byte opens | same |
| Wrong archive identity, malformed/corrupt archive, conflicting tile references | 500 `ARCHIVED_CAPTURE_CORRUPT`, zero byte opens | same |
| Physical bytes absent | 200, explicit `resource.state: missing` | 500 `ARCHIVED_CAPTURE_BYTES_MISSING` |
| Digest/size/chunk/read verification failure | 200, explicit `resource.state: error` | 500 `ARCHIVED_CAPTURE_CORRUPT` |

All error responses above are non-retryable; archive failures name safe run/artifact ids, never
filesystem paths or untrusted stored values. A resource-state 200 is not a byte success.

Pure presentation helpers may map a closed enum to an icon, token, tab order, or explanatory copy.
They may not decide whether a run is safe, complete, startable, reviewable, or actionable.

**Where the frontend keeps its half is not `state/`, and the folder name over-promises.** As built,
